title: School policies: Coverage maps do not measure strength
desc: Catalogues law-school AI policy topics and status, supporting further comparison rather than endorsing an educational approach.

kps.k: The cluster maps law-school AI policy coverage and status rather than arguing for a particular educational approach.
kps.d: AI in Legal Education: Law School Policy Archive reports 163 catalogued schools. That figure measures the archive's coverage, not the number of schools with binding AI policies. The supplied material provides an institutional inventory, not evidence of educational outcomes or agreement on how schools should regulate AI.

kps.k: The archive records variation in topic coverage and policy status, but neither measure establishes policy strength.
kps.d: Listed topic counts range from one at Yale to eight at William & Mary, with intermediate counts elsewhere. The archive labels Indiana Maurer and Stetson as guidance, Suffolk as interim, and Quinnipiac, Syracuse and UC Berkeley as in effect. It does not define the topics or explain the policies' requirements, legal force or implementation. Readers therefore cannot infer greater AI adoption or stronger governance from higher topic counts or status labels alone.

kps.k: The material supports locating policies for further comparison, not resolving debates about AI in legal education.
kps.d: Assessing permissible uses, assessment rules, enforcement or effects on professional preparation would require the underlying policy provisions and implementation evidence. No substantive disagreement or recommendation appears in the supplied excerpts. The excerpt from Foundations for Practice: The Whole Lawyer and the Character Quotient contains only institutional listings and contact information, so it adds no evidence about lawyer competencies or educational reform.

vlens.an: The source cannot be placed substantively relative to the proposition that law-school AI-policy catalogues map coverage and status without measuring policy strength or endorsing an educational approach. Its supplied excerpt consists only of law-school listings and institutional contact information; it offers no claims about AI policies, their content or force, educational outcomes, or methods for comparing policy strength. Accordingly, it neither supports nor challenges the proposition, and there is no evidence from which to identify common reasoning or internal variation within this professional voice. Because the corpus is curated and only one non-substantive source is supplied for this facet, no broader inference about access-to-justice or civil-society perspectives is warranted.

The academia-and-research source supports the cluster’s principal proposition as a descriptive inventory. The AI in Legal Education: Law School Policy Archive documents the breadth of its catalogue, variation in schools’ topic counts, and differing labels such as guidance, interim and in effect. Those data are useful for locating and comparing policies, but they do not establish policy strength, substantive requirements, implementation, educational outcomes or endorsement of any particular approach to AI in legal education. The source therefore supports the proposition’s caution against treating coverage measures as measures of governance quality. There is little internal argumentative variation because the supplied source does not advance competing recommendations; its variation is institutional and classificatory, involving different counts and policy-status labels. As this is one curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of academic or research opinion generally.

elens.an: The only source assigned to this period cannot be meaningfully positioned relative to the proposition that policy catalogues map coverage and status without measuring policy strength or endorsing an educational approach. Its supplied excerpt consists solely of law-school and institutional contact listings and contains no claims about AI policies, educational outcomes, governance strength, implementation or regulatory choices. It therefore neither corroborates nor challenges the proposition, and it adds no evidence about the distinction between policy coverage and substantive policy strength. Because this is a curated source set, this evidentiary absence should not be generalized to other sources or views from 2015–2022.

The current-wave source supports the proposition by functioning as a coverage map rather than an evaluation of law-school AI policy. It inventories 163 catalogued schools and records variation in topic counts and status labels, but provides neither the underlying policy provisions nor evidence about implementation, educational outcomes or policy effectiveness. Its material internal variation is descriptive: schools have different topic counts and are labelled as having guidance, interim policies or policies in effect. Those differences help identify policies for further comparison but do not establish stronger governance, greater AI adoption or endorsement of any educational approach. Because this time period contains one curated source, the finding should not be generalized to all current legal-education commentary.
